rationales: `<div>` is a valid HTML element.
`<span>` is a valid HTML element.
`<head>` is a valid HTML element.
`<footer>` is a valid HTML5 element, so none of the options is an incorrect tag.
CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.
Computer Style Sheets is not the expansion of CSS.
Creative Style Sheets is not the expansion of CSS.
Colorful Style Sheets is not the expansion of CSS.
`<link>` is generally used to link external resources, not to create a text hyperlink.
`<a>` creates a hyperlink, usually with an `href` attribute.
`<href>` is not an HTML element; `href` is an attribute commonly used on `<a>`.
`<nav>` identifies a section of navigation links but does not itself create a hyperlink.
`color` sets the color of text and other foreground content, not the background color.
`background-color` directly sets an element’s background color.
`bgcolor` is an obsolete HTML attribute, not the CSS property for this purpose.
`background` is a CSS shorthand that can set a background color, but `background-color` is the direct property asked for.
`class` assigns a class name and does not itself define inline styles.
`style` is the HTML attribute used to provide inline CSS declarations.
`font` is not the HTML attribute for defining inline styles.
`styles` is not the HTML attribute for defining inline styles.
A CSS rule uses a selector followed by braces containing property-value declarations separated by a colon.
This uses an equals sign instead of the required colon between a property and its value.
This uses an equals sign instead of the required colon and omits the terminating semicolon in the usual declaration syntax.
This incorrectly places a colon between the selector and its declaration block.
`/* */` is valid JavaScript block-comment syntax, so this option is also correct.
`//` is valid JavaScript single-line comment syntax, so this option is also correct.
`<!--` is recognized as a legacy single-line comment opener in JavaScript scripts, though it is not the usual comment syntax.
`/**/` is valid JavaScript block-comment syntax, so this option is also correct; the item has no unique correct answer.
The `<script>` element with a `src` attribute is the standard way to include an external JavaScript file.
`<java>` is not the standard HTML element for including JavaScript.
`<js>` is not the standard HTML element for including JavaScript.
`<code>` does not load an external JavaScript file through a `src` attribute.
`<ol>` creates an ordered list.
`<ul>` creates an unordered list.
`<li>` represents an individual list item rather than the list container.
`<list>` is not the standard HTML element for creating a list.

`<hr>` represents a thematic break and is commonly displayed as a horizontal line.
`<line>` is not the standard HTML element for displaying a horizontal line.
`<hline>` is not an HTML element.
